current_focus.summary: How the courier finds plugins, what its two doors look like, its limits, and how a store installs it.

decisions.choice: Each taking part plugin offers private POST routes courier/outbox and courier/inbox. Once a run, the courier asks each inbox what it wants (sender, topic) and its bookmark, asks the sender's outbox for news since that bookmark, and hands the batch to the inbox with the new bookmark. The receiver keeps its bookmark and ignores item ids it already has; the courier keeps nothing. Every door refuses a call that carries a person, because EmDash lets an outside request reach a private route only as a signed-in person and the courier calls with none.
decisions.question: How do plugins hand news to each other through the courier, and who keeps track of how far delivery got?
decisions.rationale: Shopify tells apps to run catch-up fetches beside its webhooks; this is that fetch, run by the store. A lost or repeated run fixes itself. Locked rule: dinkuskit plugin-communication-rule-20261122.

decisions.choice: At most 50 items per handoff, 20 handoffs per run, 8 KB per item and 20 wanted topics per receiver. A run stops at its limit and the next run, about a minute later, carries the rest.
decisions.question: How much does one courier run carry?
decisions.rationale: Shopify's REST API pages 50 records by default; WordPress runs timed jobs at most once every 60 seconds.

decisions.choice: Package @dinkuskit/courier, installed from a GitHub tag. On Cloudflare the store's once-a-minute timer runs it from the Worker's scheduled() handler; on Node the site's middleware starts a run on any visit at most once a minute, after the page. Both reach EmDash through withEmDashRuntime, so nobody needs to be signed in. A receiving plugin's admin page shows when the courier last came, or that it is missing.
decisions.question: How does a store run the courier?
decisions.rationale: The template includes it; another EmDash site adds two lines. No per-plugin change to the store.
